source.title: Label Smoothing Improves Gradient Ascent in LLM Unlearning
source.authors: Zi-Rui Pang; Hao Zheng; Zhi-Jie Deng; Ling Li; Zixin Zhong; Jia-Heng Wei

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses GA, WHP and other unlearning methods as baselines for its proposed SGA method, but does not test whether attacks recover knowledge after unlearning.
record.gate_note: The paper reports ordinary forgetting and utility metrics for unlearning baselines, including GA and WHP. It does not apply fine-tuning recovery attacks, activation ablation, quantization, or prompt-based recovery tests; its forgetting metrics are not measurements of recovery relative to a model that never saw the knowledge.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes SGA, a label-smoothed gradient-ascent unlearning method, and reports only forgetting and utility metrics for SGA and baselines on TOFU, Harry Potter and MUSE-News. It never attacks an unlearned model, so nothing tests recovery by fine-tuning (B), internal edits (C), quantization (D) or prompting (E). SGA is not shown to resist any such attack (F). It also gives no evidence on the 'attacks don't recover' half of A.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that SGA outperforms GA and is competitive with or better than other baselines across TOFU, Harry Potter and MUSE-News. They say it improves forget quality and mitigates GA's divergence and utility collapse. They draw no conclusions about recovery attacks or residual knowledge.
record.recipe_differences: SGA is a GA-based unlearning method that adds generated or selected normal data through a tunable smoothing rate; this paper evaluates it against GA and other baselines.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported SGA outcomes vary with smoothing rate, base model, and the source of normal data.

fits_no_version.finding: On MUSE-News (cited baseline values), GA drives forget-set VerbMem and KnowMem to 0.0 but also retain-set KnowMem to 0.0. WHP leaves forget-set KnowMem at 21.2 with retain-set KnowMem at 28.3. No recovery attack is applied.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-unlearning forget/retain metrics for GA and WHP on MUSE-News show forgetting-utility trade-offs. They say nothing about recoverability.

record.problems: The reported baseline outcomes use forgetting, retention, and privacy-leakage measures rather than any of the recovery attacks in the claim. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the cited MUSE-News baseline values.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version attack results were reported. SGA and other proposed-method comparisons are not included as rows because they do not test recovery after unlearning.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover the forgotten knowledge. Only post-unlearning forgetting and utility metrics are reported, with no attack.
All parts: no relearning or fine-tuning attack on unlearned models.
All parts: no activation ablation or probing of whether knowledge is blocked or deleted.
All parts: no quantization of unlearned weights.
All parts: no rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery tests.
All parts: SGA is not evaluated against any recovery attack.

record.verdict_notes: All eight rows are values the paper copied from Wang et al. 2024a (marked * in Table 3), not its own measurements. None bears on any version. Rows of SGA's own results would also bear on no version, since no attacks are run. The study is not an original source, but it gives no verdicts. SGA's own MUSE-News retain KnowMem is only 1.95, against 55.2 for the original model, and many settings collapse to 0. On Harry Potter, SGA perplexity is often enormous (e.g. 6.27e72). These numbers matter for the 'keeps general ability' clause of A, but not as a test of shallow unlearning.

versions.untested_parts: Whether simple attacks recover knowledge after unlearning; the paper evaluates neither such attacks nor targeted-knowledge accuracy against a never-trained model.
Recovery by fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples.
Recovery by activation-direction ablation or evidence that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Recovery by rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
Resistance to the recovery attacks named in the claim.
